newsitem.title: SPAIN: Renewed violence in Spain dims peace hopes.
newsitem.headline: Renewed violence in Spain dims peace hopes.

text.p: Hopes for peace in Spain's troubled Basque region dimmed on Sunday after a week in which both those for and against ETA separatist guerrilla violence turned up the heat.
Basque politicians marking the ninth anniversary on Sunday of the so-called Ajuria Enea regional peace pact were gloomy, saying the process toward "normality and peace" was stalled.

"The aims of the Ajuria Enea pact have been lost," Ramon Jauregui, socialist leader in the Basque region, told state radio. "It's obvious there is a growing pessimism in the Basque society about the end of the violence."
The pact was first signed in 1988 to show solidarity among all the Basque region parties, except ETA's political arm.
They agreed not to eliminate any option in the search for peace.

Fragile hopes for peace, which had seemed possible during a lull in violence in the last few months of 1996, were shattered last Wednesday when an army officer was shot and killed in an apparent ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) murder in Madrid.
The separatists also planted a bomb at a tax office in the north-eastern city of San Sebastian on Saturday and four smaller devices at electricity towers in the Cantabria region earlier in the week.
The bombs either exploded harmlessly or police, warned by a call in the name of ETA, were able to defuse them.
"It's time to restore the pact to the spirit it had four or five years ago..," Carlos Iturgaiz, leader of the ruling Popular Party in the Basque Country, said.
Spain's Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja says the attacks were in retaliation for police inroads into stopping growing street violence by gangs of youth supporters of ETA.

Police have been arresting members of the various so-called "Y groups" almost every day. Hooded attackers have responded by burning cars, banks and public property in daily rampages through northern cities and towns in Spain.
Jauregui said that although ETA murdered only five people last year, the lowest number since it started killing in 1968, the increased amount of street violence was disheartening.
Various attacks late on Saturday in Guipuzcoa province, a hotbed of ETA insurgence, destroyed five cars and cash machines at several banks.

Meanwhile, the Supreme Court took action on Friday against ETA's political arm and summoned the entire leadership of the Herri Batasuna (HB) political party to answer charges that they promoted violence.
The decision lifts their immunity and they will be charged with editing and distributing an ETA videotape during the campaign for a general election last March.

The video, which was played in Basque bars, clubs and schools at the start of the campaign, depicts hooded, armed rebels pleading their case. ETA has killed some 800 people in its drive for Basque independence.
Two thousand HB supporters waving red flags and chanting Socialist slogans took to the streets on Saturday to protest at the summons and to criticise "capitalist violence".
They marched through Llodio, the site of businesses linked to Cosme Delclaux, kidnapped two months ago by ETA for his failure to pay a so-called "revolutionary tax" to the rebels.
The Basque interior department said on Sunday it would seek action against HB for making threats against Basque business owners and police in the demonstration.
